newsitem.title: UK: Rand investors buy new Eurobonds to dodge losses.
newsitem.headline: Rand investors buy new Eurobonds to dodge losses.

text.p: Hard-hit investors in South African rand bonds are buying new rand Eurobonds to avoid realising losses on maturing rand debt, bankers said on Friday.

Rabobank issued a 100 million rand Eurobond on Friday, and despite the rand's continuing poor performance more deals could follow, syndicate managers said. More than 1.0 billion rand worth of Eurobonds is due to mature in the coming weeks.

"Some investors will invest redemption proceeds into smaller new issues rather than take the currency loss they are now exposed to," said a syndicate manager at a European bank involved in the Eurorand sector.
"The currency loss on the very first rand issues (launched in 1995) is about 30 percent in dollar terms, and it's a comparable figure against marks," he said.

Gerry Moes, director at Hambros Bank, lead manager of Friday's rand Eurobond, said, "Upcoming redemptions, a total of 1.1 billion rand, are expected to trigger further buying interest stemming from reinvestment flows."
The rand started 1997 under pressure, losing two cents to hit 4.70 per dollar. At 1435 GMT it was quoted at 4.6985/35.

The rand saw prolonged stability against the dollar at around 3.65 after the financial rand was abolished in March 1995. But last February it started a dramatic slide, falling by more than 25 percent in less than three months.

Economic and political uncertainty also continues to dog the country. Newspapers on Friday speculated Finance Minister Trevor Manuel would be moved in a cabinet reshuffle, to be replaced by minister of trade and industry Alec Erwin.
But there is unlikely to be enough new rand issuance in the weeks ahead to match the funds generated by maturing bonds, so at least some of the proceeds will probably move elsewhere, dealers said.
"Unless we see signigicant developments in South Africa soon, some investors will just accept their losses and reinvest in other currencies," said a debt trader.
The Czech crown sector is currently a favoured high-yielder, with three bonds for a total of 3.5 billion crowns launched already this year.
